prompt.context: Leslie Knope has been recently elected to the Town Council of Pawnee, Indiana. During her campaign, she promised the citizens of Pawnee that she would build a beautiful new park. The town's budget, however, does not have the funding to fulfill Leslie's ambitious promise. Leslie wants your advice on how to proceed and determine if and how it's possible to build her park.
prompt.question: How should Leslie proceed? Determine if and how it is possible to build the park, given the town's budget constraints.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the park cost?
What is the Parks Department annual budget?
clarifying_info.a: The Parks Department annual budget is approximately $5 million.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other relevant campaign promises?
clarifying_info.a: There are no other relevant campaign promises.

clarifying_info.q: Can the town run a budget deficit?
clarifying_info.a: The town is not allowed to run a budget deficit and typically returns surplus funds to taxpayers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the status of other departments' budgets?
clarifying_info.a: Leslie doesn't know the status of other departments' budgets.

exhibits.title: 2009 and 2013 Budgets
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts comparing Pawnee's departmental budgets in 2009 (non-personnel only) and 2013 (total). The 2009 chart shows a total of $85M; the 2013 chart shows a total of $100M. Several department values are shown while a few are left blank (marked with '?') for the candidate to calculate.

framework: Revenues: identify all revenue sources available to the town (taxes, fees, state/federal grants, donations)
Expenditures: examine current town spending by department and category (personnel, equipment, etc.) to find savings
Analysis of Alternatives: consider building something smaller (shade garden, smaller park), improving existing parks instead
Other considerations: timeline for delivery and political impact of failing to deliver on the campaign promise

questions.prompt: Walk through your initial framework for how Leslie can find funding to build the park.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates structure the problem MECE: revenue side (new/increased taxes, fees, grants, donations) vs. expenditure side (cutting costs across departments). They prioritize the two most impactful areas, explain why, and propose to dive into one. They should also raise alternatives (smaller park, improving existing parks) and other considerations (timeline, political risk of non-delivery).

questions.prompt: The client wants to focus on town expenditures. What categories and types of expenses exist, and how can Pawnee reduce them?
questions.guidance: Pure brainstorming — no wrong answers. Strong responses are creative, plausible, and highly structured in buckets (e.g., Personnel: hiring freezes, reduce overtime, renegotiate contracts; Infrastructure/Maintenance: defer non-critical repairs, renegotiate vendor contracts; Utilities: energy efficiency, renegotiate rates; Administration: reduce headcount, consolidate departments; Public Services: reduce frequency or scope of services). Exceptional candidates add depth after each 'What else?' and eventually propose to explore one area in detail.

questions.prompt: Review Exhibit 1. What do you observe about Pawnee's budget from 2009 to 2013, and what are the key numbers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) The utilities budget has roughly doubled while other departments remained relatively stable. (2) Pawnee's overall budget capacity appears strained — total went from $85M (2009 non-personnel) to $100M (2013 all-in), suggesting the town is spending more. Candidate must remember Parks = $5M from the clarifying questions. For 2009, the data shown is non-personnel only; personnel expenses equal 50% of the listed amounts for 2009 (so multiply each 2009 figure by 1.5 to get total). Key numbers to derive: Parks 2013 = $5M (from memory); Public Works 2013 = $100M - $13.75M - $15M - $11M - $6M - (45%x$100M) - $5M = $100M - $13.75M - $15M - $11M - $6M - $45M - $5M = $4.25M; Utilities 2009 total = $3M x 1.5 = ... wait, Utilities 2009 non-personnel is derived as $85M - $5M - $6M - $11M - $8M - $5M - $48M = $2M non-personnel; total 2009 Utilities = $2M x 1.5 = $3M. The doubling of Utilities from $3M (2009) to $6M (2013) is the key insight.

math.setup: Derive missing 2013 values: Total 2013 = $100M; Schools = 45% x $100M = $45M; Parks = $5M (given); so Public Works = $100M - $13.75M - $15M - $11M - $6M - $45M - $5M. Derive Utilities 2009: $85M total non-personnel minus all listed departments. Then apply 1.5x multiplier for personnel.
math.answer: Public Works 2013 = $4.25M; Utilities 2009 total = $3M; Utilities budget doubled from 2009 to 2013

questions.prompt: Since 2009, Pawnee replaced old bulbs with SuperNova bulbs, which have not reduced electricity as marketed. Pawnee is considering replacing half the public lights (keeping SuperNovas in street lights) with Eco lights that consume 40% of the electricity of a SuperNova. The bulb replacement costs 0.5% of the total 2013 budget (one-time cost). Should Pawnee proceed?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual electricity savings from switching, compare to one-time cost, and connect the net savings back to the park-building goal. Strong candidates note that the savings are almost enough to fund the park on their own. Exceptional candidates confidently defend their math if challenged and suggest ways to close the remaining gap.

math.setup: Electricity = 2/3 of utilities budget = 2/3 x $6M. Pawnee keeps SuperNovas in street lights (50% of all public lights). The other 50% is replaced with Eco lights that use 40% of SuperNova electricity (saving 60%). One-time cost = 0.5% x $100M total 2013 budget.
steps: Lights being replaced = 50% of all public lights
Electricity savings from replaced lights = 50% x 60% x $4M = 2/3 x 1/2 x 3/5 x $6M = 6/30 x $6M = $1.2M
math.answer: Annual electricity savings = $1.2M; one-time cost = $500K; net savings = $700K. Yes, Pawnee should proceed. The $700K net savings is nearly enough to fund the $750K park.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some categories and types of expenses in a town budget, and how might Pawnee reduce them?

categories.name: Personnel
ideas: Hiring freeze
Reduce overtime pay
Renegotiate union contracts
Voluntary furloughs or early retirement programs
Reduce benefits (healthcare plan tier, pension contributions)

categories.name: Utilities and Energy
ideas: Switch to energy-efficient lighting (directly relevant to the case)
Renegotiate utility supply contracts
Install smart meters or timers on public facilities
Solar panels on municipal buildings

categories.name: Infrastructure and Maintenance
ideas: Defer non-critical road or building repairs
Consolidate maintenance contracts
Reduce frequency of routine maintenance where safe

categories.name: Administration
ideas: Consolidate back-office functions across departments
Reduce printing and paper use
Switch to open-source or lower-cost software
Reduce number of administrative layers

categories.name: Public Services
ideas: Reduce hours of non-essential services (libraries, community centers)
Consolidate service delivery routes
Partner with neighboring towns for shared services
Outsource select functions to lower-cost providers

categories.name: Procurement and Contracts
ideas: Renegotiate vendor and supplier contracts
Consolidate purchasing to gain volume discounts
Use competitive bidding for all major contracts

categories.name: Capital Expenditures
ideas: Delay non-critical capital projects
Sell unused municipal property or equipment
Lease instead of buy equipment where cheaper

recommendation: Pawnee should proceed with replacing the non-street-light SuperNova bulbs with Eco lights, generating $700K in net first-year savings and $1.2M in annual savings thereafter — nearly enough to fund the $750K park
The remaining ~$50K gap can be closed through small additional expenditure cuts, a grant application, or a minor fee or donation campaign
risks: The bulb replacement is a one-time fix; if other utility costs continue rising, further structural budget reform will be needed
Cutting departmental budgets may face political resistance or service-quality backlash
If the park is not built, there is political risk to Leslie's credibility and mandate
next_steps: Authorize the Eco light bulb replacement project immediately to capture savings
Identify a supplementary funding source (state/federal parks grant, donations, minor fee) to close the ~$50K gap
Commission a broader expenditure review across all departments, particularly the doubling utilities budget, to ensure long-term fiscal health
